A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeStyle study. The main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and matchable across the additions, relocations, and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 32 LLMs across seven jailbreak benchmarks, controlled fine-tuning experiments, and SafeStyle comparisons, with additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and reports additional model evaluations, alternative-judge checks, controlled style experiments, and SafeStyle robustness results.

M1.justification: SafeStyle retains the same intervention: incorporate 50 safety examples augmented to match fine-tuning styles. Section 5.2 also retains GPT-4o style extraction and frequency-based sampling of ten bigrams for real-world datasets. The additional evaluations introduce no method component, objective, or procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: The seven jailbreak benchmarks, Alpaca/Dolly training data, AlpacaEval, HumanEval, and six principal styles are retained. Appendix C.2 extends SafeStyle's evaluation from matched training/attack styles to a scenario including attack styles unseen during its fine-tuning. News/legal analyses already appeared in v2.

E2.justification: The comparator set remains No Defense, Vanilla, PTST, SPPFT, Constrained, and Paraphrase. The new defense comparisons reuse this set. DeepSeek models are evaluated backbones, while Llama-Guard and Qwen3Guard are judges, not additional defense baselines.

E3.justification: The survey expands from 32 to 36 models by adding three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models and GPT-4o-mini; SafeStyle is additionally tested on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. New evaluation designs introduce two alternative judges, 50 manually curated intents with synthetic styles, semantic/syntactic overlap controls, cross-style averages, and joint safety/utility rankings. Existing fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial checks of judge dependence and benchmark-extraction artifacts in Appendix A.2, semantic versus syntactic trigger effects in Figure 11, SafeStyle robustness to unseen attack styles in Table 10, and safety/utility ranking analysis in Table 9. The earlier news/legal extensions, utility curves, and HumanEval check are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 adds a paired t-test for ASR inflation, reporting p = 0.0002. Appendix A.2 newly reports Cohen's kappa agreement with alternative judges: 0.767 and 0.858. The existing three-run mean-reporting statement is unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: All 336 numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. The expanded survey reports inflation in 32/36 models instead of 28/32, and Figure 3's attention correlation changes from 0.571 to 0.456 under the expanded model set. New Tables 4 and 7–10 and Figure 11 add extensive results; for example, Table 8 reports SafeStyle delta ASR of -0.007 for news and -0.004 for legal, the latter tied with Constrained. Figure 9 updates length/complexity correlations to 0.125/0.076, although Appendix A.3 retains v2's 0.129/0.078.

T1.justification: The definitions of ASR inflation and attention difference remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The new semantic-backdoor discussion is an empirical interpretation, and the added rankings and agreement measures are evaluation analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: styles inflate ASR, superficial style alignment creates safety vulnerabilities, and style-matched safety data mitigates them while preserving utility. Updating the survey from 32 to 36 models expands supporting evidence without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands mechanism and applicability interpretation: Appendix B.2 characterizes the effect as semantic style compliance rather than exact-token triggering, and Appendix C.2 discusses protection when attacker styles differ from training. New qualifications explain the stress-test role of poetry/Shakespeare styles. Section 6 expands the limitations discussion and recommends benchmarking malicious intent and style as separate evaluation dimensions.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 newly discloses that identical-intent exclusions account for 4% of queries. The appendices document construction of the new curated-intent and prefix-overlap controls. The original hyperparameter grid, LLaMA-Factory implementation, eight A100 GPUs, safety-data provenance, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: New citations cover DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3Guard, BackdoorLLM and a backdoor survey, linguistic style research, and hierarchical safety benchmarks such as SALAD-Bench and SafeDialBench. These support the added controls and benchmark recommendations; the central positioning relative to alignment and fine-tuning defenses remains stable.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained, with targeted rewrites and expanded explanations. Conclusion becomes Discussion with Conclusion, Future Works, and Broader Impacts paragraphs; Appendix A gains a subsection and B.2 is retitled. Acknowledgements and the ICLR publication header are also added.

P2.justification: v3 adds three figures for alternative judges and semantic/syntactic controls, plus five tables for controlled styles, judge comparisons, reasoning-model results, rankings, and cross-style evaluation. Existing survey/correlation plots gain model entries and revised legends. Main tables and retained appendix displays are relocated, producing a substantial expansion of the visual evidence while preserving the overall design.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: alternative judges test dependence on GPT-4o, controlled experiments test benchmark artifacts and exact-wording explanations, and Table 10 evaluates SafeStyle beyond matching attack styles. These additions substantially strengthen the central empirical argument and practical applicability while preserving the original comparisons. Appendix A.3's stale correlation values introduce a small reporting defect, but the corresponding qualitative trends remain unchanged.
